passages.t: A failing king, two captains, and a lame boy
passages.happening:
When Ish-bosheth hears that Abner has died in Hebron, ‘he lost courage, and all Israel was dismayed’ (verse 1).

Two men serve him as leaders of raiding parties, the brothers Baanah and Rechab, sons of Rimmon from Beeroth in Benjamin. The narrator explains that the people of Beeroth had fled to Gittaim, where they still live as foreigners (verses 2-3).

Then, before the story goes on, it stops to name one more of Saul's family. Jonathan had a son, lame in his feet. He was five years old when the news of Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. ‘His nurse picked him up and fled, but as she was hurrying to escape, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
This is the end of Ish-bosheth's two years at Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, somewhere near the end of the first decade of the tenth century BC; the exact dates are uncertain. Abner was the last strong man of Saul's house. Without him, its king has no courage and no support.

Beeroth was one of the four towns of the Gibeonites, the people who made a treaty with Joshua, and it was later counted as part of Benjamin. The note that its people fled suggests some upheaval that drove them out. Some readers connect it with Saul's attempt to wipe out the Gibeonites (21:1-2), which might give these brothers a reason to hate Saul's house, but the text does not say so.

The story of Mephibosheth breaks in at a tense moment, just after the killers are named and before they strike. Its place makes a point. Saul's house, which once had a king a head taller than everyone, is now represented by a lame child. His injury came from someone else's panic, not from anything he did. He is the last male of Saul's line with a claim to the throne, and he will matter later, when David seeks to show kindness to Jonathan's family (chapter 9). First Chronicles calls him Merib-baal, and as with Ish-bosheth, most scholars think the scribes of Samuel put bosheth, shame, in place of baal.
passages.later:
Beeroth was among the towns that made peace with Joshua by a trick (Joshua 9:17), and later it was listed in Benjamin's land: ‘Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth’ (Joshua 18:25).

Chronicles gives Jonathan's son his other name: ‘The son of Jonathan: Merib-baal’ (1 Chronicles 8:34).
passages.asks: Mephibosheth's whole life was shaped by a fall that was not his fault. Ask whose life near you carries the marks of someone else's crisis. And ask what it would look like to treat them as a person and not as a problem.

passages.happening:
Rechab and Baanah come to Ish-bosheth's house ‘in the heat of the day, while the king was taking his midday nap’ (verse 5). They go inside as if to fetch wheat, and they kill him on his bed. They cut off his head and travel all night through the Arabah to Hebron.

They bring the head to David: “Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy who sought your life. Today the LORD has granted vengeance to my lord the king against Saul and his offspring” (verse 8).

David answers with an oath: ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life from all distress’ (verse 9). He reminds them of the man who brought word of Saul's death, expecting a reward, and was put to death at Ziklag. How much more, he says, when wicked men kill a righteous man in his own house and on his own bed (verse 11). David's young men kill Rechab and Baanah. They cut off their hands and feet and hang their bodies by the pool in Hebron. Ish-bosheth's head is buried in Abner's tomb at Hebron (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The midday rest in the heat of the day was a normal custom, and a house would be quiet then. The killers walk in as if they had come for grain, which shows how easily they moved in the king's house. To kill a man on his own bed, in his own house, was a particularly treacherous act, a breach of the safety everyone expected at home. The narrator tells the murder twice (verses 6 and 7), which slows the scene and lets its cruelty sink in.

Bringing an enemy's head to a king was a way of proving a kill and claiming a reward, as David himself once brought Goliath's head before Saul. The brothers even dress the murder in religious words: the LORD has given the king vengeance. David will not have it.

His oath is the heart of the chapter. The LORD, he says, has redeemed his life from all distress. He has never needed anyone to rescue him by murder. And he argues from the lesser to the greater: if the man who only claimed to have killed Saul died for it, how much more these men. He calls Ish-bosheth a righteous man. The word means innocent here: Ish-bosheth had done nothing to deserve death at the hands of his own officers.

The chapter is framed by hands. It opens with Ish-bosheth's hands growing weak, which is the Hebrew picture behind losing courage (verse 1), and it ends with the murderers' hands cut off (verse 12). Burying Ish-bosheth's head in Abner's tomb gave him an honorable burial beside the commander who had made him king.
passages.later:
David's sentence rests on Israel's oldest law about blood: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind” (Genesis 9:6). The law of Moses said the same of a murderer: ‘the murderer must surely be put to death’ (Numbers 35:16).

It also limited what could be done to the body of an executed man: ‘you must not leave the body on the tree overnight, but you must be sure to bury him that day’ (Deuteronomy 21:23).
passages.hard:
Was David's punishment of Rechab and Baanah just, and why were their bodies cut and displayed?

By the standards of Israel's law, the penalty for planned murder was death (Numbers 35:16-21), and these men had killed a sleeping king in his own house. The cutting and the public display are harder for modern readers. In the ancient world such displays were a common way to show the reason for a punishment and to deter others, and here the hands that killed and the feet that ran with the head were singled out. The law limited the exposure of an executed body to a single day, and nothing suggests David broke that limit.

Some readers see the harsh treatment as political theater, David showing in public that he had no part in the murder. Others see ordinary justice for its time. The text does not present it as a model for all times. What it does show is David's resolve that his kingdom would not be built on innocent blood.
passages.asks: The killers called their murder the LORD's vengeance. Ask where you have heard God's name used to dress up something cruel. And ask what it would mean for you, like David, to refuse a gain that came by someone else's wrong.
